title: Notes Java Multithreading Using Runnable Interface

items.question: Q1. What are the ways of creating threads in Java?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: Independent instructions are executed by threads, and there are two ways to create the threads for them. In the first way the class that holds the instructions extends the Thread class. In the second way the class implements the Runnable interface. In both ways the independent instructions are placed inside the run() method.

items.question: Q2. What is the Runnable interface?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: Runnable is an interface of the java.lang package. It is a functional interface, which means that it has exactly one abstract method, and that method is run(). A class that implements Runnable gives the body of run(), and the body contains the independent instructions that are to be executed in a thread.

items.question: Q3. What is the relationship between the Thread class and the Runnable interface?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: The Thread class itself implements the Runnable interface, and this is how the run() method is available in Thread. Opening the Thread class in an IDE such as Eclipse shows implements Runnable in its declaration. The Thread class also has a constructor that accepts a reference of a Runnable object, so any object of a class that implements Runnable can be handed over to a Thread object.

items.question: Q4. How is a class changed from extending Thread to implementing Runnable?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: Only the declaration changes. The words extends Thread are replaced with implements Runnable, and the run() method with its independent instructions stays the same. For example, class PrintingNumbers extends Thread becomes class PrintingNumbers implements Runnable. The word implements means that the class provides the body for the abstract method of the interface. Since the class no longer extends Thread, it does not inherit anything from the Thread class, including the start() method.

items.question: Q5. Why can start() not be called on an object of a class that only implements Runnable?
Q6. What are the steps for achieving multithreading?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: There are four steps. Step 1 is to identify the independent instructions that have to execute at the same time. Step 2 is to put those instructions inside the run() method, either by extending the Thread class or by implementing the Runnable interface. Step 3 is to create the thread, which has a small stack of its own: this is done by creating an object of the class that extends Thread, or, when the class only implements Runnable, by creating a Thread object. Step 4 is to call start() on the thread object, so that the thread begins to execute run().

Q9. What happens when start() is called on a Thread object that was created with a Runnable object?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: The thread gets its own stack, and the run() method of the Runnable object that was passed to the Thread constructor is executed on that stack. The run() method of the Thread class calls the run() method of the Runnable object. In the program above, the run() frame of PrintingCharacters is placed in the stack of t1, and the run() frame of PrintingNumbers is placed in the stack of t2.

items.question: Q10. What happens in memory when a program creates threads using Runnable objects?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: The program starts with the main stack, and the main method frame is placed in it. Objects are created in the heap. The statements new PrintingCharacters() and new PrintingNumbers() create objects in the heap only. These classes implement Runnable and do not extend Thread, so no new stack comes with these objects. The statements new Thread(pc) and new Thread(pn) create two Thread objects in the heap, and each of them represents a thread with a small stack of its own, apart from the main stack. The variables t1 and t2 refer to these Thread objects. After start() is called on them, the run() frames are placed in their stacks. The main stack and the two small stacks are then executed concurrently. When the first way is used, the object of the class that extends Thread is itself the thread, and the small stack comes with that object.

items.question: Q11. How is the time of a process shared among its threads, and what is concurrency?
items.answer: Answer: Ans: A process gets a fixed amount of execution time, and that time is divided among its threads. For example, if a process has 20 seconds and four threads, each thread gets 5 seconds. When the time of a thread is over, it is stopped and the next thread is given its turn. The stopped thread gets its turn again later and continues from the point where it stopped. This switching happens so fast that the threads seem to run at the same time. This way of executing is called concurrent execution, and multithreading is therefore also called concurrent programming. Because the switching is decided by the system, the order in which the statements of different threads are printed can change between runs.
